pages.title: Sullivan Center
pages.text:
Sullivan Center (formerly known as the Schlesinger & Mayer Building, Carson Pirie Scott Building, or Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Store) is a 12-story building at State and Madison streets in Chicago, Illinois, United States. Opened in phases between 1899 and 1907, the building was designed by Louis Sullivan, originally for retail firm Schlesinger & Mayer, and was Sullivan's last large commercial building. For much of the 20th century, it housed the flagship store of Carson Pirie Scott (Carson's), which also occupied other properties on the same block. The building is a Chicago Landmark and National Historic Landmark and is part of the Loop Retail Historic District.
Schlesinger & Mayer previously occupied the Bowen Building on the same site and expanded it gradually during the 1880s and early 1890s. They originally commissioned Sullivan in the 1890s to expand the existing building before hiring him to complete a new structure. Sullivan oversaw both the original 1899 building and a 1903 annex. The building was sold in 1904 to H. G. Selfridge & Co., who sold the building to Otto Young and leased it to Carson's. Subsequent additions were completed by D. H. Burnham & Company in 1906–1907 and Holabird & Root in 1961. Carson's occupied the store until 2006, during which it gradually acquired both the building and the site. Following renovations in the late 2000s, it became Sullivan Center, an office complex.
The main elevations of the building's facade on State and Madison streets, are connected by a curved corner. On each elevation, piers divide the facade into bays with wide Chicago windows. The lowest two stories are clad with decorative cast iron, with an entrance at the corner and large windows on either elevation. The windows on the upper stories are framed by white terracotta bands. The foundation includes a mixture of caissons and pilings, while the superstructure consists of cast iron and steel columns, which support terracotta floor slabs. The store's interior layout was arranged to maximize selling space, with open plan spaces between the columns. Sullivan Center was Sullivan's last large major commercial design. It has been praised over the years for its engineering and architecture, despite mixed views of the exterior design details.


== Site ==
Sullivan Center, a.k.a. the Carson Pirie Scott Building, is located at 1 South State Street at the southeast corner of East Madison Street in the Loop section of downtown Chicago, Illinois, United States. It is part of a larger complex once operated by Carson, Pirie and Scott (colloquially Carson's), which occupied much of the city block bounded by State Street to the west, Madison Street to the north, Wabash Avenue to the east, and Monroe Street to the south. An alley runs from Madison to Monroe streets. Adjoining the building above Wabash Avenue is the Chicago "L"'s elevated Loop. The Chicago Building and One South Dearborn are immediately across State Street to the west, and the Haskell-Barker-Atwater Buildings and Silversmith Hotel are on the same block to the east.
The intersection of Madison and State streets is the zero-point baseline for the city's address grid system and dates from the original 1830s plat of Chicago. Because of this, both streets were misaligned where they crossed each other; this influenced the design of the Bowen Building, the previous building on the site.


=== Previous building ===
State Street's commercial strip was leveled during the Chicago Fire of 1871 and then rebuilt. Among the structures built after the fire was the Bowen Building at the southwest corner of State and Madison, designed by William Boyington and completed in 1872. This building originally housed clothing firm Clement, Morton & Co. Clement, Morton originally leased the Bowen Building for five years, but moved to another building in 1875 before the lease had expired. The next occupant, the Wilson Sewing Machine Company, moved into the building in 1876. The third occupant was Schlesinger & Meyer, a dry-goods store, which opened in April 1881. The land itself was acquired by Levi Z. Leiter in 1878 and leased to the building's successive owners under a leasehold agreement.
The Bowen Building originally measured six stories high and 60 by 80 feet (18 by 24 m) across, with the wider frontage on Madison Street. The misalignment of State and Madison streets had created a "prominent projection" at their southeast corner; Boyington took advantage of this by adding a rounded pavilion at the corner. The corner pavilion was topped by a circular dome with dormers, while the rest of the building had a mansard roof. Cornices ran across the facade, splitting it into two tiers of double-height columns and pilasters. Inside, the building had steam heat and elevators, both technologically advanced for the time. Adjoining it were several buildings of different heights.


== Development ==


=== Background ===
The idea for Sullivan Center arose following repeated expansions of the Bowen Building, whose final tenant, Schlesinger & Mayer, was operated by Leopold Schlesinger and David Mayer. Both German immigrants to the US, they had met while working together prior to the Chicago Fire. The company was founded in 1872  and occupied a space covering 2,500 square feet (230 m2), Schlesinger in particular had become familiar with the work of Adler & Sullivan, the architectural partnership of Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan, in the 1880s, and he hired them to design his house on Michigan Avenue in 1884. Schlesinger & Mayer quintupled the Bowen Building's area from 32,000 to 160,000 square feet (3,000 to 14,900 m2) between 1881 and 1895 by leasing and remodeling space in adjacent buildings.


==== 1881–1895: Early leases and expansions ====
In 1885, Schlesinger & Mayer leased 133–135 State Street immediately south of the Bowen Building, which gave the company a total of 60,000 square feet (5,600 m2). Leiter attempted to evict the firm that year because of a dispute over the ground-lease payments. Schlesinger & Mayer ended up buying the building (but not the land) in 1886, and a judge ruled against Leiter in 1889. Adler & Sullivan were hired in 1890 to replace the Bowen Building's mansard roof and dome with two additional stories. Sullivan was asked to redesign three bays, with the rest to follow if Schlesinger & Mayer liked his work. That February, Schlesinger & Mayer leased two properties south of the existing store, at 137–139 State Street. A boiler plant was added in conjunction with this annex. Two additional buildings at 141–143 State Street were acquired in 1891, increasing the frontage there to 200 feet (61 m). The four State Street properties formed an L-shaped assemblage, as the newly leased lots at 137–143 State extended 160 feet (49 m) eastward from State Street, while the two buildings to the north extended only 80 feet (24 m) eastward.

After leasing 141–143 State, Schlesinger & Mayer wanted Adler & Sullivan to remodel the State Street buildings as a single structure with a unified facade; sources disagree on whether the enlarged building was to be six or eight stories high. Minimal interior modifications were needed because the floor levels of all four buildings were at the same heights. The renovations would have included an elaborate entrance on State Street, plans for which were announced in 1892. No action was taken for several years, during which Adler and Sullivan dissolved their partnership, forcing Schlesinger & Mayer to pick between the two men. Schlesinger & Mayer ultimately hired Sullivan because of his reputation designing artistic buildings. Frank Lloyd Wright, a onetime draftsman at Adler & Sullivan, later said that most of their clients had instead stayed with Adler.


==== 1896–1897 expansion ====

Schlesinger & Mayer's site on State Street was among the most valuable in Chicago by the early 1890s. One block east, the Union Elevated Railroad (later part of the Chicago "L") was constructing its Loop above Wabash Avenue. Several retailers on State Street had acquired land on Wabash Avenue to cater to the riders who were expected to use the elevated. Other retailers nearby—who, like Schlesinger & Mayer, leased the land under their buildings and had high ground-lease payments—were rebuilding their stores to attract customers.
In May 1896, Schlesinger & Mayer signed a 99-year lease for two lots on Wabash Avenue owned by the Barker family. The next month, the company signed another 99-year lease with Frederick T. Haskell for two adjacent sites to the south, giving it an 80-by-171-foot (24 by 52 m) assemblage at 141–147 Wabash Avenue. Schlesinger & Mayer commissioned Sullivan to design a ten-story steel structure. The company set a $100,000 budget for the building, which was to be connected by a footbridge to its existing State Street buildings. Work on the Barker site at 141–143 Wabash was underway by August 1896, in anticipation of a September opening. The existing four-story structure was to be remodeled, forming the base of the ten-story building, but only the lowest two floors were ultimately renovated. Schlesinger & Mayer also negotiated to lease two stories in an adjacent building at 135–139 Wabash. The Haskell lease at 145–147 Wabash was not finalized until early 1897.
Sullivan expanded 137–143 State to six stories in 1896, following the original early-1890s plans for these sites. This renovation included an elaborate French cafe. After these modifications were completed in 1897, the building measured eight bays wide on State Street and four on Madison Street, in addition to the Wabash Avenue property.  Sullivan also designed a pedestrian bridge connecting 141–143 Wabash's second floor to the elevated Loop's brand-new Madison/Wabash station. Schlesinger & Mayer and Union Elevated agreed to the footbridge in May 1897, but just as the bridge was being completed, the city halted work on November 20. Overnight, 200 workers secretly completed the bridge, which opened the next day. The bridge had elaborate metalwork, steel girders, and glass walls and was similar in design to an overpass in Paris, but was later removed. Schlesinger & Mayer leased 145 State Street from Burley & Co. in 1897, adding 30 feet (9.1 m) to the State Street frontage south of the existing lots. This lease did not take effect until May 1900 when the existing tenants moved out.


=== New building ===
The rest of Schlesinger & Mayer's original plans, including the 10-story building on Wabash Avenue, were never carried out. The new storefront at 141–143 Wabash was the only pre-1898 design that survived the store's redevelopment over the next decade. The Lansing Journal later said that Schlesinger & Mayer's central location had attracted so many customers, "a mammoth new store has become necessary for their business".


==== First phase ====
In early 1898, Leiter gave Schlesinger & Mayer a 99-year ground lease on the Bowen Building property for $11.088 million, a record for any property in Chicago. The lease mandated the complete redevelopment of the site within ten years and that any new building cost at least $600,000. Schlesinger & Meyer also bought multiple adjacent buildings, including the properties already leased by the store, for the new project. Sullivan drew up two designs, rising 10 and 12 stories but otherwise identical, with elaborate bronze storefronts on the lowest two stories and a white marble facade above. That May, news media reported that the 12-story design would be built for $1 million, while sketches in the Chicago Daily Tribune showed the 10-story plan. Contrasting with Sullivan's previous rectangular work, the building was to contain a rounded corner at State and Madison, evoking the Bowen Building's old curve; the curve was shaped as an octagon at its base. The plans, exhibited at the Chicago Architectural Club that year, were so extravagant that they elicited skepticism.
Leiter sold the Bowen Building site that July to Marshall Field's department store, operated by Leiter's former business partner Marshall Field. By then, Schlesinger & Mayer had hired Adler to design the store's electrical plant, disregarding the possibility of conflict with Sullivan. After a period of vacillation regarding the building's size, Schlesinger & Mayer decided to erect the building in phases, starting with property on Madison Street. The company also directed Sullivan to shorten the building to nine floors. It received a construction permit for the first phase on Madison Street in November 1898, covering a 140-by-182-foot (43 by 55 m) site. The first phase occupied only part of its lot, measuring three bays wide; this allowed the existing Bowen Building and its annexes to remain open temporarily. Sullivan had completed his working drawings by the end of December, by which point work was to begin in early 1899. Continued confusion arose when Schlesinger & Mayer's indecision over the building's height, which was ultimately finalized at nine stories to comply with Chicago's 130-foot (40 m) height limit.
The plans were finalized in April 1899; the building was downsized because Schlesinger & Mayer had not acquired as much land as expected. This revised plan was to cost $600,000. Land clearing at 50–56 Madison Street began on May 1, and the firm simultaneously leased temporary space at 133–139 Wabash. That July, Schlesinger & Mayer paid the Chicago government $500 for permission to protrude the storefront bay outward. Work on the new building was rushed to minimize lost profits; by October, the new building's first phase had topped out. The first phase was open at the end of the year, having cost over $330,000. By then, the site was among the highest-valued in Chicago, at $159.68 per square foot ($1,718.8/m2). The opening of the Schlesinger & Mayer Building's first phase coincided with the completion of two other Sullivan projects: the Gage Group Buildings and the Bayard–Condict Building.


==== Second phase ====

Eugene S. Pike, who owned the Bowen Building's leasehold, sued Schlesinger & Mayer in February 1900, claiming the firm was "ruining the building" by removing stairs, walls, elevators, and machinery. A judge placed an injunction restricting further renovations that April. Merchant Otto Young, who had acquired land immediately to the south at 145–153 State Street, announced the next year that Schlesinger & Mayer planned to develop a building there. Schlesinger & Mayer wished to resume construction after the Chicago City Council voted in March 1902 to increase height limits to 260 feet (79 m). The company sought to build a 280-foot-tall (85 m) tower was unsuccessful in securing a further height increase.
Henry Siegel, the executive of Siegel, Cooper & Co., acquired Schlesinger's share of the company in June 1902 following months of negotiations. This acquisition increased Schlesinger & Mayer's assets to $6.5 million; at the time, the building's full construction cost was estimated at $1–2 million. Siegel, Cooper & Co. decided to proceed with the second phase, and Schlesinger & Mayer took out a $3 million mortgage loan on the property in August. Sullivan drew up drawings for an annex at the corner of State and Madison streets. The annex, covering 180 by 70 feet (55 by 21 m), was similar in design to the first phase but had 12 stories. Schlesinger & Mayer initially intended to also expand the first phase from 9 to 12 stories but learned that its foundations were too weak. The final design was nearly identical to Sullivan's original 1898 plans, except for the base and top three stories.
The George A. Fuller Company was hired as the general contractor for the second phase. In October, workers began constructing caissons for the second phase's foundation under the existing buildings, which remained in operation, to avoid interfering with the store's holiday window displays. Due to the constrained space, only six caissons were laid at a time. Two lifts were installed to extract debris, but to avoid turning away visitors, no supplies could be stored on the street. The foundations were completed in January 1903 and cost only about $8,000 more than comparable foundations built on empty sites. The Fuller Company was rehired for the second phase's superstructure. The northern section at the corner was to be built by May, followed by the southern section that October. Schlesinger & Mayer moved to the new building's first phase on Madison Street and the older buildings on State Street, which flanked the corner lot.
After the corner had been razed, work on the second phase's northern section began on January 15, 1903. Steelwork was being installed by January 25, and it took twelve days to construct the floor slabs. The corner section was finished on April 25 and opened on May 11. Land clearing for the second phase's southern section began in May, immediately after the northern section opened. The framework had been built by July. The next month, laborers went on strike to protest Fuller Construction's refusal to hire carpenters for the building's falsework; the strike ended after two weeks. The southern section opened on October 12, 1903, giving the building a frontage of 180 feet (55 m) on State and 145 feet (44 m) on State Street. Though the building had cost $1.65 million to date, the interior was still incomplete. The second phase's construction had caused $300,000 in lost revenue between January and May 1903 alone. Sullivan also redesigned the Wabash Avenue buildings that year. When the second phase opened, Schlesinger & Mayer gave tours of the mechanical system.


==== Ownership changes ====
Meanwhile, Schlesinger & Mayer's monetary shortfalls had prompted Mayer to seek further land for expansion, as well as more radical ideas such as merging with rival department store Carson Pirie Scott (colloquially Carson's). The company had leased 155 State Street from Adolf Kraus in August 1903 and it leased the adjacent Columbus Club property on Monroe Street, the next month. The company, needing to expand its offices quickly, evicted a jeweler who had been subleasing 145 State. The firm unsuccessfully attempted to buy Young's lease at 145–153 State, which separated the new building from the Columbus Club and 155 State. By early 1904, Mayer no longer wanted to acquire additional land and was looking to sell the building and leaseholds.
Department store operator Harry Selfridge bought the new building, the leaseholds, and all of Schlesinger & Mayer's other assets in May 1904. He paid $5 million, far more than what equivalent real estate across State Street would have cost. The building became a Selfridge & Co. store that June, and Selfridge sold the building to Young that month for $1.485 million, occupying it under a leaseback agreement. Field continued to own the land. Selfridge was unable to obtain 145–153 State, and the leases of 155 State and the Columbus Club also fell through.
After eight weeks of ownership, Selfridge sold the building's lease and the store's assets to Carson's that August for a net profit of $400,000. The lease on Carson's previous flagship store at the Reliance Building was about to expire, influencing its decision to buy the Selfridge's building. Carson's agreed to pay Young $196,000 annually for the building, which was renamed the Carson Pirie Scott Building. The company relocated there on September 19, 1904; it was the final relocation for Carson's Chicago flagship, which had moved nearly a dozen times in a half-century of business.


==== Third phase ====
Soon after acquiring the building, Carson's sought to expand it southward, but it did not hire Sullivan for unknown reasons. D. H. Burnham & Company—the architectural firm of Daniel Burnham, who had designed the Reliance Building—was hired to design the third phase of the Carson Pirie Scott Building. The annex, measuring five bays wide, was to be built at 145–153 State. Carson's subleased the site from Young in January 1905, paying $346,000 annually. Carson's and Young agreed to construct a 12-story building with foundations strong enough for 18 stories, continuing the exterior design of the first two phases. Construction was to be postponed until the next year, and several months elapsed before Burnham began working on the design. That August, the city government notified Carson's that the curved corner entrance protruded onto the street and was likely subject to rent payments.
Field died in January 1906, bequeathing his land to the Field Museum of Natural History. Shortly afterward, Burnham & Co. subcontracted the masonry and foundation work to Thompson–Starrett Company. Carson's received a construction permit for the annex in mid-April, and demolition work began on May 1. At the time, the annex had an estimated cost of $850,000. Young died that year, but his will precluded the trustees of his estate from selling the building until at least ten years after the death of his daughter Julia. Under his will, rental income from the building went to his daughters. The original Carson Pirie Scott Building's third and final phase ultimately opened in October 1907, providing additional space for men's, women's, and children's clothing departments.


== Operational history ==


=== 20th century ===


==== Late 1900s to late 1920s: Expansion ====
Initially, Carson's used its storefront windows for elaborate displays. The city government directed Carson's to remove protruding signage from the Madison Street facade in 1909. as part of a signage ban along that street. In 1912, the Crozer family—the legal owner of the lots at 145–153 State, by then renamed 25–29 South State Street—sold these parcels to the Field estate.
In 1922, Carson's bought the Thomas Church Building at 32–34 South Wabash Avenue, adjoining its existing Wabash Avenue frontage. Carson's obtained the Mentor Building at State and Monroe two years later. This gave the company full control of State Street's eastern frontage between Madison and Monroe streets. Following these land acquisitions, Carson's contemplated expanding the existing building farther south. Concurrently, Burnham & Co. was erecting the Wabash Monroe Building, at the northwest corner of Wabash Avenue and Monroe Street on the same block, for another developer. The company leased several floors in the Wabash Monroe Building for its men's store in late 1926; at the time, several of Carson's competitors had men's departments facing Wabash Avenue, while the men's store still occupied the building on State Street. Carson's had leased the entirety of the Wabash Monroe Building by that December, and it also evicted the Church Building's tenants to provide space for the men's store.
The men's store moved to the Wabash Monroe Building in July 1927. Carson's also moved several other departments to the new building, allowing the company to renovate the older building. The main entrance was relocated southward, away from the curved corner, The interior was reconfigured to provide wider aisles. Several existing departments were enlarged, and new counters were built around existing columns to take advantage of the open-plan interiors. A footbridge was built to connect the shoe departments in the Carson Pirie Scott and Wabash Monroe buildings. Carson's postponed its plans for a southward expansion of the original building, instead leasing out the Mentor Building.


==== Early 1930s to early 1950s ====
Carson's had acquired two further plots on Wabash Avenue by 1930, connecting the interiors of these buildings and remodeling their storefronts. By then, the original Carson Pirie Scott Building on State Street and the store's Wabash Avenue expansions, which were offset from each other, covered much of the block. In 1935, Carson's announced plans to spend $1.25–1.5 million on renovations, including heating, air conditioning, and elevators. Escalators were also added, necessitating the rearrangement of interior spaces, including new diagonal aisles on the second floor. A plaque to World War I soldiers was dedicated at the building in 1938, and four budget-merchandise departments opened two years later. When the State Street subway was proposed in 1941, Carson's received permission to construct an entrance from the subway (between Washington and Monroe stations, which shared a continuous platform) to the original Carson Pirie Scott Building. The subway entrance opened in 1944.
By the mid-1940s, Carson's sought to expand its building, though World War II-era material restrictions prevented work from beginning immediately. Carson's received a permit in 1947 to expand into the north–south alley running midblock between Madison and Monroe streets. The next year, the facade decorations were removed from the top floors of Sullivan's sections. Carson's also announced plans for another building on Monroe Street, consisting of modifications to an existing 10-story building there. The Monroe expansion opened in 1950. The downtown Chicago buildings were Carson's only store location until 1952, when the company opened its first branch. Carson's leased space in the building to Childs & Wood for an insurance bureau the next year. By then, the original building was known as the North State Street Building.


==== Mid-1950s to late 1960s: Further expansion ====

In 1954, Carson's proposed buying the original building at State and Madison from Otto Young's estate for $6,321,503, but the trustees could not sell the building without court permission because Julia Young was still alive. If acquisition were not possible and Young's trustees could not lower the rent, Carson's threatened to relocate. Carson's submitted an updated bid of $7.25 million in January 1955, but federal judge Michael L. Igoe restarted the bidding process the next month. In response, Carson's proposed expanding the Wabash Avenue properties—forming an L shape around the original building—for $5 million. Carson's also sought to sell the lease, which ran five more years. When a New York company offered $7.5 million for the building that July, Igoe withheld approval of the bid contingent on Carson's ability to match the order. After Carson's agreed to pay that amount, Igoe gave Carson's the right to buy the building.
Carson's finalized its purchase in October 1955, paying about 25% of the cost in cash and taking out a mortgage for the remaining amount. The same year, Carson's announced plans to condense its selling areas, since it no longer needed to reserve space in the Wabash Avenue properties for a potential relocation. The top floors of the original building and the Wabash Monroe Building were converted to offices, and new air conditioning and escalators were added on the original building's lowest eight floors. The original decorations at the corner entrance, on State and Madison, were removed or concealed. The renovation program was half-complete by 1958, at which point sales departments had been consolidated in the basement through seventh stories; many of the departments had also been rearranged between different floors. The Heather House restaurant opened on the eighth floor in 1959. Despite Carson's rapid growth in the suburbs, its downtown store was still its primary operation.
By 1960, Carson's had acquired three buildings south of the Carson Pirie Scott Building, having leased the sites for several years. That July, Carson's announced plans to spend $2 million on an eight-story annex south of the existing building, designed by Holabird & Root and spanning 59,500 square feet (5,530 m2). The annex was one of several ongoing major expansions of department stores on State Street during that time. By then, the store occupied over 1 million square feet (93,000 m2) on the block, but the company was considering leasing out space in its adjacent buildings. The annex was finished by 1961, and O'Connor & Goldberg leased a shoe store on the annex's lower floors. Carson's also restored other parts of its existing structures and continued to seek additional property on the same block during the decade. Large parts of the Carson Pirie Scott Building were damaged by arson in 1968, causing $20 million in damage; some departments reopened quickly, but the flagship store still lost money due to the fire.


==== 1970s to 1990s ====

A Honey Bear Farm gourmet shop opened at the building in 1970. During that decade, the Field Museum still owned the site, with the United Methodist Church and the Northern Trust Company as co-owners. Carson's bought the Field Museum's section of the land in 1978 for $2 million, gaining full control of the property. The land acquisition ensured that ownership of the building would not revert to the landowner when the leasehold expired. Concurrently, Carson's had announced plans in 1977 for a renovation of the building's first floor, part of a wider-ranging initiative to rehabilitate State Street. Architect John Vinci was hired to oversee the renovation, which involved cleaning the upper facade and repainting the base. The work also involved restoring the original ornamentation in the corner entrance's vestibule, which was rededicated in mid-1979.
The first floor was renovated in 1984. Carson's also spent $2–3 million converting the basement into a Corporate Level store for women, which opened that August. The next year, Carson's divided the second floor into 30 small apparel shops, renovated the men's departments, and opened a Corporate Level men's store next to the women's store. Carson's evicted O'Connor & Goldberg from the State Street annex in 1986 to expand its own departments, and a grocery store opened at the building the following year. By the late 1980s, the site occupied a blighted portion of State Street, and many nearby upscale stores had moved to the Magnificent Mile on Michigan Avenue. Bergner's, which acquired Carson's in 1989, considered closing and redeveloping the Carson's flagship building.

pages.text:
Louis Henry Sullivan (September 3, 1856 – April 14, 1924) was an American architect, and has been called a "father of skyscrapers" and "father of modernism". He was an influential architect of the Chicago School, a mentor to Frank Lloyd Wright, and an inspiration to the Chicago group of architects who have come to be known as the Prairie School. Along with Wright and Henry Hobson Richardson, Sullivan is one of "the recognized trinity of American architecture." The phrase "form follows function" is attributed to him; it encapsulated earlier theories of architecture and he applied them to the modern age of the skyscraper. In 1944, Sullivan was the second architect to posthumously receive the AIA Gold Medal.


== Early life and career ==
Sullivan was born to a Swiss-born mother, Andrienne née  List (who had emigrated to Boston from Geneva with her parents and two siblings, Jenny, b. 1836, and Jules, b. 1841) and an Irish-born father, Patrick Sullivan. Both had immigrated to the United States in the late 1840s. He learned that he could both graduate from high school a year early and bypass the first two years at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology by passing a series of examinations. Entering MIT at the age of sixteen, Sullivan studied architecture there briefly. After one year of study, he moved to Philadelphia and took a job with architect Frank Furness.
The Depression of 1873 dried up much of Furness's work, and he was forced to let Sullivan go. Sullivan moved to Chicago in 1873 to take part in the building boom following the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. He worked for William LeBaron Jenney, the architect often credited with erecting the first steel frame building. After less than a year with Jenney, Sullivan moved to Paris and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts for a year. He returned to Chicago and began work for the firm of Joseph S. Johnston & John Edelman as a draftsman. Johnston & Edleman were commissioned for the design of the Moody Tabernacle, and tasked Sullivan with the design of the interior decorative fresco secco stencils (stencil technique applied on dry plaster). In 1879 Dankmar Adler hired Sullivan. A year later, Sullivan became a partner in Adler's firm. The time at Adler & Sullivan marked the beginning of Sullivan's most productive years.
Adler and Sullivan initially achieved fame as theater architects. While most of their theaters were in Chicago, their fame won commissions as far west as Pueblo, Colorado, and Seattle, Washington (unbuilt). The culminating project of this phase of the firm's history was the 1889 Auditorium Building (1886–90, opened in stages) in Chicago, an extraordinary mixed-use building that included not only a 4,200-seat theater, but also a hotel and an office building with a 17-story tower and commercial storefronts at the ground level of the building, fronting Congress and Wabash Avenues. After 1889 the firm became known for their office buildings, particularly the 1891 Wainwright Building in St. Louis and the Schiller (later Garrick) Building and theater (1890) in Chicago. Other buildings often noted include the Chicago Stock Exchange Building (1894), the Guaranty Building (also known as the Prudential Building) of 1895–96 in Buffalo, New York, and the 1899–1904 Carson Pirie Scott Department Store by Sullivan on State Street in Chicago.


== Sullivan and the steel high-rise ==

Prior to the late nineteenth century, the weight of a multi-story building had to be supported principally by the strength of its walls. The taller the building, the more strain is placed on the lower sections of the building; since there were clear engineering limits to the weight such "load-bearing" walls could sustain, tall designs meant massively thick walls on the ground floors, and definite limits on the building's height.
The development of cheap, versatile steel in the second half of the nineteenth century changed those rules. America was in the midst of rapid social and economic growth that made for great opportunities in architectural design. A much more urbanized society was forming and the society called out for new, larger buildings. The mass production of steel was the main driving force behind the ability to build skyscrapers during the mid-1880s. By assembling a framework of steel girders, architects and builders could create tall, slender buildings with a strong and relatively lightweight steel skeleton. The rest of the building elements—walls, floors, ceilings, and windows—were suspended from the skeleton, which carried the weight. This new way of constructing buildings, so-called "column-frame" construction, pushed them up rather than out. The steel weight-bearing frame allowed not just taller buildings, but permitted much larger windows, which meant more daylight reaching interior spaces. Interior walls became thinner, which created more usable (and rentable) floor space.
Chicago's Monadnock Building (not designed by Sullivan) straddles this remarkable moment of transition: the northern half of the building, finished in 1891, is of load-bearing construction, while the southern half, finished only two years later, is of column-frame construction. While experiments in this new technology were taking place in many cities, Chicago was the crucial laboratory. Industrial capital and civic pride drove a surge of new construction throughout the city's downtown in the wake of the 1871 fire.
The technical limits of weight-bearing masonry had formal and structural constraints which were remedied by Sullivan. None of the historical precedents were necessarily followed, causing a sort of literary, and technical crisis. Sullivan addressed the crisis by embracing the changes that came with the steel frame, creating a grammar of form for the high rise (base, shaft, and cornice), simplifying the appearance of the building by breaking away from historical styles, using his own intricate floral designs, in vertical bands, to draw the eye upward and to emphasize the vertical form of the building, and relating the shape of the building to its specific purpose. Such innovations were unique, and commercially successful.
In 1896, Louis Sullivan wrote:

It is the pervading law of all things organic and inorganic, of all things physical and metaphysical, of all things human, and all things super-human, of all true manifestations of the head, of the heart, of the soul, that the life is recognizable in its expression, that form ever follows function. This is the law. (italics in original)

"Form follows function" would become one of the prevailing tenets of modern architects.
Sullivan attributed the concept to Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect, engineer, and author, who first asserted in his book, De architectura (On architecture), that a structure must exhibit the three qualities of firmitas, utilitas, venustas – that is, it must be "solid, useful, beautiful." This credo, which placed the demands of practical use equal to aesthetics, later would be taken by influential designers to imply that decorative elements, which architects call "ornament", were superfluous in modern buildings, but Sullivan neither thought nor designed along such dogmatic lines during the peak of his career and this credo never put one concept above another. While his buildings could be spare and crisp in their principal masses, he often punctuated their plain surfaces with eruptions of lush Art Nouveau or Celtic Revival decorations, usually cast in iron or terra cotta, and ranging from organic forms, such as vines and ivy, to more geometric designs and interlace, inspired by his Irish design heritage. Terra cotta is lighter and easier to work with than stone masonry. Sullivan used it in his architecture because it had a malleability that was appropriate for his ornament. Probably the most famous example of ornament used by Sullivan is the writhing green ironwork that covers the entrance canopies of the Carson Pirie Scott store on south State Street.
Such ornaments, often executed by the younger draftsmen in Sullivan's employ, eventually would become Sullivan's trademark; to students of architecture, they are instantly recognizable as his signature.
Another signature element of Sullivan's work is the massive, semi-circular arch. Sullivan employed such arches throughout his career—in shaping entrances, in framing windows, or as interior design.
All of these elements are found in Sullivan's widely admired Guaranty Building, which he designed while partnered with Adler. Completed in 1895, this office building in Buffalo, New York is in the Palazzo style, visibly divided into three "zones" of design: a plain, wide-windowed base for the ground-level shops; the main office block, with vertical ribbons of masonry rising unimpeded across nine upper floors to emphasize the building's height; and an ornamented cornice perforated by round windows at the roof level, where the building's mechanical units (such as the elevator motors) were housed. The cornice is covered by Sullivan's trademark Art Nouveau vines and each ground-floor entrance is topped by a semi-circular arch.
Because Sullivan's remarkable accomplishments in design and construction occurred at such a critical time in architectural history, he often has been described as the "father" of the American skyscraper. But many architects had been building skyscrapers before or as contemporaries of Sullivan; they were designed as an expression of new technology. Chicago was replete with extraordinary designers and builders in the late years of the nineteenth century, including Sullivan's partner, Dankmar Adler, as well as Daniel Burnham and John Wellborn Root. Root was one of the builders of the Monadnock Building (see above). That and another Root design, the Masonic Temple Tower (both in Chicago), are cited by many as the originators of skyscraper aesthetics of bearing wall and column-frame construction, respectively.


== Later career and decline ==

In 1890, Sullivan was one of the ten U.S. architects, five from the east and five from the west, chosen to build a major structure for the "White City", the World's Columbian Exposition, held in Chicago in 1893. Sullivan's massive Transportation Building and huge arched "Golden Door" stood out as the only building not of the current Beaux-Arts style, and with the only multicolored facade in the entire White City. Sullivan and fair director Daniel Burnham were vocal about their displeasure with each other. Sullivan later claimed (1922) that the fair set the course of American architecture back "for half a century from its date, if not longer." His was the only building to receive extensive recognition outside America, receiving three medals from the French-based Union Centrale des Arts Decoratifs the following year.
Like all American architects, Adler and Sullivan suffered a precipitous decline in their practice with the onset of the Panic of 1893. According to Charles Bebb, who was working in the office at that time, Adler borrowed money to try to keep employees on the payroll. By 1894, however, in the face of continuing financial distress with no relief in sight, Adler and Sullivan dissolved their partnership. The Guaranty Building was considered the last major project of the firm.
By both temperament and connections, Adler had been the one who brought in new business to the partnership, and following the rupture Sullivan received few large commissions after the Carson Pirie Scott Department Store. He went into a twenty-year-long financial and emotional decline, beset by a shortage of commissions, chronic financial problems, and alcoholism. He obtained a few commissions for small-town Midwestern banks (see below), wrote books, and in 1922 appeared as a critic of Raymond Hood's winning entry for the Tribune Tower competition.
In 1922, Sullivan was paid $100 a month to write an autobiography in installments to be published in the journal for the American Institute of Architects. Sullivan worked on the series with Journal editor Charles Harris Whitaker, who advised he "plot out the material by periods." The Autobiography of an Idea began its publication in the June 1922 Journal for the American Institute of Architects and upon its conclusion was published as a book.
He died in a Chicago hotel room on April 14, 1924. He left a wife, Mary Azona Hattabaugh, from whom he was separated. A modest headstone marks his final resting spot in Graceland Cemetery in Chicago's Uptown and Lake View neighborhood. Later, a monument was erected in Sullivan's honor, a few feet from his headstone.


== Legacy ==
Sullivan's legacy is contradictory. Some consider him the first modernist. His forward-looking designs clearly anticipate some issues and solutions of Modernism; however, his embrace of ornament makes his contribution distinct from the Modern Movement that coalesced in the 1920s and became known as the "International Style". Sullivan's built work expresses the appeal of his incredible designs: the vertical bands on the Wainwright Building, the burst of welcoming Art Nouveau ironwork on the corner entrance of the Carson Pirie Scott store, the (lost) terra cotta griffins and porthole windows on the Union Trust building, and the white angels of the Bayard Building, Sullivan's only work in New York City. Except for some designs by his longtime draftsman George Grant Elmslie, and the occasional tribute to Sullivan such as Schmidt, Garden & Martin's First National Bank in Pueblo, Colorado (built across the street from Adler and Sullivan's Pueblo Opera House), his style is unique. A visit to the preserved Chicago Stock Exchange trading floor, now at The Art Institute of Chicago, is proof of the immediate and visceral power of the ornament that he used so selectively.
After his death Sullivan was referred to as a bold architect: "Boldly he challenged the whole theory of copying and imitating, and the catchword of "precedent", declaring that architecture was naturally a living and creative art." James Marston Fitch wrote that Sullivan "was quick to see the advantages in other men's work, and quick to adapt them to his own uses . . . He was a man in search of an architectural idiom which would be, not his own personal property, but that of the American people."  Sullivan believed that architecture was a manifestation of a culture, its people, its needs, and its values. The architect, Sullivan told the Chicago Architectural Club in 1899, "is and imperatively shall be an interpreter of the national life of his time."
Original drawings and other archival materials from Sullivan are held by the Ryerson & Burnham Libraries in the Art Institute of Chicago and by the drawings and archives department in the Avery Architectural and Fine Arts Library at Columbia University. Fragments of Sullivan buildings also are held in many fine art and design museums around the world.


== Preservation ==
During the postwar era of urban renewal, Sullivan's works fell into disfavor, and many were demolished. In the 1970s, growing public concern for these buildings finally resulted in many being saved. The most vocal voice was Richard Nickel, who organized protests against the demolition of architecturally significant buildings. Nickel and others sometimes rescued decorative elements from condemned buildings, sneaking in during demolition. Nickel died inside Sullivan's Stock Exchange building while trying to retrieve some elements, when a floor above him collapsed. Nickel had compiled extensive research on Adler and Sullivan and their many architectural commissions, which he intended to publish in book form.
After Nickel's death, in 1972, the Richard Nickel Committee was formed, to arrange for completion of his book, which was published in 2010. The book features all 256 commissions of Adler and Sullivan. The extensive archive of photographs and research that underpinned the book was donated to the Ryerson and Burnham Libraries at The Art Institute of Chicago. More than 1,300 photographs may be viewed on their website and more than 15,000 photographs are part of the collection at The Art Institute of Chicago. As finally published, the book, The Complete Architecture of Adler & Sullivan, was authored by Richard Nickel, Aaron Siskind, John Vinci, and Ward Miller.

Another champion of Sullivan's legacy was the architect Crombie Taylor (1907–1991), of Crombie Taylor Associates. After working in Chicago, where he headed the famous "Institute of Design" (later known as the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT)) in the 1950s and early 1960s, he moved to Southern California. He led the effort to save the Van Allen Building in Clinton, Iowa from demolition. Taylor, acting as an aesthetic consultant, worked on the renovation of the Auditorium Building (now Roosevelt University) in Chicago.
When he read an article about the planned demolition in Clinton, he uprooted his family from their home in southern California and moved them to Iowa. With the vision of a destination neighborhood comparable to Oak Park, Illinois, he set about creating a nonprofit to save the building, and was successful in doing so. Another advocate for the buildings of both Sullivan and Wright was Jack Randall, who led an effort to save the Wainwright Building in St. Louis, Missouri at a very critical time. He relocated his family to Buffalo, New York to save Sullivan's Guaranty Building and Frank Lloyd Wright's Darwin Martin House from possible demolition. His efforts were successful in both St. Louis and Buffalo.
A collection of architectural ornaments designed by Sullivan is on permanent display at Lovejoy Library at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. The St. Louis Art Museum also has Sullivan architectural elements displayed. The City Museum in St. Louis has a large collection of Sullivan ornamentation on display, including a cornice from the demolished Chicago Stock Exchange, 29 feet long on one side, 13 feet on another, and nine feet high.
The Guaranty Building Interpretive Center in Buffalo, on the first floor of the building now owned and occupied by the law firm Hodgson Russ, LLP, opened in 2017. The exhibit space was financed by Hodgson Russ and co-designed by Flynn Battaglia Architects and Hadley Exhibits. It features a scale model of the building by David J. Carli, professor of engineering at the State University of New York at Alfred. The center's exhibits were donated to Preservation Buffalo Niagara. The center, the only museum dedicated to Sullivan, is open to the public.


== Sullivan in Ayn Rand's The Fountainhead ==
That the fictional character of Henry Cameron in Ayn Rand's 1943 novel The Fountainhead was similar to the real-life Sullivan was noted, if only in passing, by at least one journalist contemporary to the book.
Although Rand's journal notes contain in toto only some 50 lines directly referring to Sullivan, it is clear from her mention of Sullivan's Autobiography of an Idea (1924) in her 25th-anniversary introduction to her earlier novel We the Living (first published in 1936, and unrelated to architecture) that she was intimately familiar with his life and career. The term "the Fountainhead", which appears nowhere in Rand's novel proper, is found twice (as "the fountainhead" and later as "the fountain head") in Sullivan's autobiography, both times used metaphorically.
The fictional Cameron is, like Sullivan – whose physical description he matches – a great innovative skyscraper pioneer late in the nineteenth century who dies impoverished and embittered in the mid-1920s. Cameron's rapid decline is explicitly attributed to the wave of classical Greco-Roman revivalism in architecture in the wake of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, just as Sullivan in his autobiography attributed his own downfall to the same event.
The major difference between novel and real life was in the chronology of Cameron's relation with his protégé Howard Roark, the novel's hero, who eventually goes on to redeem his vision. That Roark's uncompromising individualism and his innovative organic style in architecture were drawn from the life and work of Frank Lloyd Wright is clear from Rand's journal notes, her correspondence, and various contemporary accounts. In the novel, however, the 23-year-old Roark, a generation younger than the real-life Wright, becomes Cameron's protégé in the early 1920s, when Sullivan was long in decline.
The young Wright, by contrast, was Sullivan's protégé for seven years, beginning in 1887, when Sullivan was at the height of his fame and power. The two architects would sever their ties in 1894 due to Sullivan's angry reaction to Wright's moonlighting in breach of his contract with Sullivan, but Wright continued to call Sullivan "lieber Meister" ("beloved Master") for the rest of his life. After decades of estrangement, Wright would again become close to the now-destitute Sullivan in the early 1920s, the time when Roark first comes under the likewise impoverished Cameron's tutelage in the novel. Wright, however, was now in his fifties. Nevertheless, both the young Roark and middle-aged Wright had in common at that time that they both faced a decade of struggle ahead. After the triumphs earlier in his career, Wright came increasingly to be viewed as a has-been, until he experienced a renaissance in the latter half of the 1930s with such projects as Fallingwater and the Johnson Wax Headquarters.

=== Banks ===

Sulliven's later output consisted primarily of a series of small bank and commercial buildings in the Midwest. When the director of a bank that was considering hiring him asked Sullivan why they should engage him at a cost higher than the bids received for a conventional Neo-Classic styled building from other architects, Sullivan is reported to have replied, "A thousand architects could design those buildings. Only I can design this one." He got the job. These commissions are collectively referred to as Sullivan's "Jewel Boxes", and all still stand.

National Farmers' Bank of Owatonna, Owatonna, Minnesota (1908)
Peoples Savings Bank, Cedar Rapids, Iowa (1912)
Henry Adams Building, Algona, Iowa (1913)

Home Building Association Company, Newark, Ohio (1914)
Purdue State Bank, West Lafayette, Indiana (1914)
People's Federal Savings and Loan Association, Sidney, Ohio (1918)
